article.abstract: Fluid therapy is ubiquitous in the intensive care unit (ICU) but carries risks, especially in mechanically ventilated patients. Contemporary global practice across dose, indication, and type is unknown. To characterize ICU fluid practices in mechanically ventilated adults. International prospective observational cohort study between April 2024 and July 2025, across 206 ICUs in 41 countries on 6 continents. Consecutive adult patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation within 3 days of ICU admission and ventilated 24 hours or more. Exclusion criteria were age younger than 16 years and transfer under mechanical ventilation from another ICU. Fluid volume, indication, and type after intubation. Key measures included (1) total infused volume and daily fluid balance over 7 days after intubation; (2) the indication for fluid therapy over the first 3 days after intubation; (3) the proportion of total administered fluid volume attributable to each fluid type over the first 3 days after intubation. Among 2454 patients analyzed (median age, 63 years [IQR, 49-73 years]; 63.6% [1560] male), median daily fluid input peaked on day 1 at 3.0 L (IQR, 2.2-4.0 L) and declined to 2.6 L (IQR, 1.8-3.5 L) through day 6. Daily fluid balance (median, 0.9 L; IQR, 0.1-1.9 L on day 1) decreased to less than 0.3 L (IQR, -0.5 to 1.2 L) by day 3 and remained near-neutral through day 6. Maintenance and replacement fluids (to meet daily requirements and to correct ongoing losses; 31.9%) and creep fluids (to deliver medications and maintain catheter patency; 30.9%) were the primary indications, whereas resuscitation (to restore circulating blood volume; 16.0%) accounted for a smaller proportion. Isotonic balanced crystalloids (48.9%) and isotonic saline (0.9% sodium chloride) (27.0%) were common; colloids were rare (1.3%). Substantial between-site variation persisted after adjustment for case-mix. In this prospective international cohort study, fluid therapy varied widely among mechanically ventilated critically ill patients, with maintenance and creep fluids-rather than resuscitation fluids-accounting for most total volume.

article.abstract: Oliguria is a key prognostic indicator of acute kidney injury (AKI), yet the consensus definition (< 0.5 mL/kg/hr) is increasingly questioned. We aimed to determine thresholds of lowest mean diuresis (LMD) associated with AKI, chronic kidney disease (CKD), and mortality. Retrospective observational study. Uppsala University Hospital ICU, Sweden. A total of 4999 adults (≥ 18 yr) without preexisting CKD admitted to the ICU between 2017 and 2024. None. LMD was calculated over 3, 6, 12, and 24 hours (LMD3h-LMD24h). Generalized additive models were used, adjusting for Simplified Acute Physiology Score 3 estimated mortality ratio and gender. Outcomes were AKI within 7 days of LMD (Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes creatinine criteria), incident CKD after ICU discharge, and 90-day mortality. All LMD time frames were significantly associated with AKI, CKD, and death (p < 0.0001). Thresholds for AKI were 0.43, 0.41, 0.42, and 0.53 mL/kg/hr; for CKD, 0.21, 0.21, 0.31, and 0.43 mL/kg/hr; and for mortality 0.16, 0.18, 0.24, and 0.39 across LMD3h-LMD24h. The risk of mortality or persistent kidney injury, reflected by incident CKD, increases at a lower urine output threshold than the current AKI definition. These findings support the idea of filtration deficit, urine output, and tissue injury as different dimensions of AKI and should influence future AKI definitions.

article.abstract: Chlorhexidine (CHX) has been a long-standing component of oral-care bundles for preventing ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP), but recent evidence has questioned its benefit in non-cardiac-surgery ICU. We evaluated whether adding 0.12% CHX to standardized oral-care bundle provides incremental benefit in a mixed medical ICU. We conducted a prospective, pragmatic cluster-randomized crossover (AB/BA) trial in six adult medical ICUs of a single tertiary-care academic hospital in Bhubaneswar, India. ICUs were randomized as three ICUs of two Period of 9 months with the multicomponent oral-care bundle without chlorhexidine and three with the same bundle plus 0.12% chlorhexidine with a 1-month wash-in and re-training interval. Consecutive adults ventilated for ≥ 48 h were included. The primary outcome was VAP incidence density (Clinical Pulmonary Infection Score (CPIS) > 6) as per 1,000 ventilator-days. Secondary outcomes were 28-day all-cause mortality, duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU length of stay, 28- day ventilator-free days, Beck Oral Assessment Scale (BOAS) and Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool (CPOT) scores. The primary model was a population-averaged Poisson generalized estimating equation (GEE) and adjustment for treatment, period, sequence, age, sex, APACHE II, and SOFA. A total of 1,035 patients (637 No CHX, 398 CHX) accrued 10,024 ventilator-days (5,918 vs. 4,106). Groups were well balanced at baseline (mean age ≈ 55 years; APACHE II ≈ 19.6; SOFA ≈ 13.4). VAP occurred in 100/5,918 ventilator-days (16.9 per 1,000) vs. 77/4,106 (18.8 per 1,000) (No CHX vs. CHX). The adjusted Poisson incidence rate ratio was 1.08 (95% CI 0.84-1.38; p = 0.56). 28-day mortality was 28.7% vs. 26.4% (no CHX vs. CHX) (adjusted OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.65-1.15; p = 0.33). ICU length of stay was longer in the CHX arm (adjusted mean difference + 0.89 days, 95% CI + 0.19 to + 1.58; p = 0.013). BOAS and CPOT scores did not differ. In this trial, adding 0.12% chlorhexidine to a standardized oral-care bundle did not reduce VAP incidence density or 28-day mortality and was associated with a modest increase in ICU length of stay. Routine CHX use provided no clear incremental benefit in a mixed medical ICU population. Clinical Trials Regisrty- India (CTRI) identifier [CTRI/2024/02/062201], registered [01 February 2024].

article.abstract: Mucormycosis is a rare but life-threatening invasive fungal infection that primarily affects immunocompromised patients. Data on its presentation, management, and prognosis in the intensive care unit setting remain scarce. We aimed to evaluate 90-day mortality and to explore clinical, microbiological, therapeutic, and immunological factors associated with outcome in critically ill patients with mucormycosis. This retrospective multicenter cohort study included patients diagnosed with mucormycosis and admitted to the ICUs of the Hospices Civils de Lyon between January 2014 and July 2023. Patients were identified through mycological records and hospital discharge codes. Univariable analysis and multivariable Cox model were performed to identify factors associated with 90-day mortality. Among 43 patients included, hematological malignancy and trauma were the most common underlying conditions (26% each), followed by solid organ transplantation (21%), and burns (16%). Cutaneous forms (49%) predominated, especially among trauma and burn patients, while pulmonary and rhinocerebral forms were mostly observed in previously immunocompromised individuals. The number of mucormycosis diagnoses increased nearly threefold over the study period, paralleling the implementation of Mucorales-specific polymerase chain reaction. Antifungal therapy was initiated in 39 patients (91%); first-line treatment was liposomal amphotericin B in 32 (74%), at a median maximum dose of 7.5 [3.5-9.4] mg/kg/day, and 12 (28%) received a combination therapy. The 90-day mortality was 47%. In the multivariable Cox model, older age, hematological malignancy, and a higher Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score at diagnosis were independently associated with mortality, while lower liposomal amphotericin B dosing was associated with mortality in univariable analysis. In eight patients without previous immunosuppression and uncontrolled disease, immune monitoring was performed and revealed decreased monocyte HLA-DR expression at 4556 [4194-6936] Ab/c, in favor of injury-induced immunosuppression. Among them, six patients received interferon-gamma as immunotherapy; four responded immunologically and survived. Mucormycosis in critically ill patients is associated with high mortality, particularly in those with hematological malignancies. Polymerase chain reaction-based diagnostics may allow earlier detection, and immune monitoring could help identify high-risk patients, particularly in trauma and burn settings.

authors: PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients without ARDS (PRoVENT), PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients in Middle-income Countries (PRoVENT-iMiC), and Extubation strategies in Neuro-ICU patients and associations with Outcomes (ENIO) investigators

article.abstract: To describe ventilatory management in neurocritical care and non-neurocritical care patients and determine whether specific ventilator settings are associated with development of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and mortality in neurocritical care patients. The primary endpoint was a diagnosis of ARDS after initiation of invasive ventilation; one secondary endpoint was ICU mortality. Post hoc pooled analysis of harmonized individual patient data from three recent prospective observational studies combined into the PRIME database. PRIME is a harmonized pooled database comprising individual patient data from three recent prospective observational studies on ventilatory management in critically ill patients: "PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients without ARDS" (PRoVENT), "PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients in Middle-income Countries" (PRoVENT-iMiC), and "Extubation strategies in Neuro-ICU patients and associations with Outcomes" (ENIO). We excluded patients with ARDS at the start of ventilation. Demographic and clinical characteristics, ventilator settings, respiratory variables, arterial blood gas values, and clinical outcomes were extracted from the harmonized PRIME database. Derived ventilation parameters included tidal volume normalized to predicted body weight, driving pressure, respiratory system compliance, mechanical power, ventilatory ratio, and Pao2/Fio2 ratio. This analysis included 3848 patients, including 1702 neurocritical care and 1920 non-neurocritical care patients. Based on recorded ventilatory variables, neurocritical care patients received lower median tidal volumes (Vts), positive end-expiratory pressure, and Fio2. They had lower median driving pressure (ΔP), mechanical power (MP) of ventilation, and ventilatory ratio, as well as higher respiratory system compliance compared with non-neurocritical care patients. These differences were consistently observed at both assessed time points. ARDS was diagnosed more frequently in neurocritical care patients than in non-neurocritical care patients (8.7% vs. 3.9%; p < 0.001), while ICU mortality was lower (14.3% vs. 22.8%; p < 0.001). Among neurocritical care patients, those who developed ARDS were ventilated with lower median Vt and higher Fio2 and had higher median ΔP and MP. Vt normalized for predicted body weight in neurocritical care patients was independently associated with the development of ARDS. In this cohort, ventilatory management at the initial and 48-hour assessments differed between neurocritical care and non-neurocritical care patients, particularly with respect to key ventilator settings like Vt, positive end-expiratory pressure, and Fio2. In neurocritical care patients, ARDS was more often diagnosed than in non-neurocritical care patients.

article.abstract: Automated pupillometry quantifies the pupillary light reflex in acute brain injury. The neurological pupil index (NPi) is the established composite index and carries prognostic value. A second index from a different device, the quantitative pupil index (QPi), has recently become available, but whether it conveys equivalent information in non-anoxic acute brain injury is unknown. LYNX was a prospective cohort study in three European intensive care units (September 2022-July 2024). Consecutive adults with traumatic brain injury, subarachnoid or intracerebral haemorrhage, or ischaemic stroke ventilated for more than 12 h were enrolled and followed for 6 months. Paired NPi (NPi-300) and QPi (NeuroLight) measurements were obtained at least every 6 h to day 7. Ancillary cohorts of healthy volunteers (dark vs. bright light) and surgical patients (before and after sufentanil and propofol) were also studied. The primary outcome was the correlation between the two indices; secondary outcomes were their association with intracranial hypertension and unfavourable 6-month outcome (Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended ≤ 4). Values below 3 were considered abnormal, with QPi thresholds of 2 and 4 as sensitivity analyses; multivariable models were adjusted for age, sex, admission Glasgow Coma Scale score and focal deficit. Among 108 patients (median age 57 years [IQR 44-67], 60.2% male), 7089 paired measurements were obtained. The two indices were moderately to strongly correlated (r = 0.717, 95% CI 0.705-0.730). Each 10-percentage-point increase in abnormal values independently predicted unfavourable outcome (NPi: OR 1.49, 95% CI 1.09-2.04, p = 0.013; QPi: OR 1.76, 95% CI 1.31-2.37, p < 0.001). QPi was associated with intracranial hypertension (OR 1.38, 95% CI 1.04-1.82, p = 0.025), whereas NPi was not. Ambient lighting and contralateral eye opening had no meaningful effect in 75 volunteers. In 20 sedated non-brain-injured patients, propofol reduced QPi to a median of 1 (IQR 1-3) and NPi to 4.0 (IQR 3.6-4.3). NPi and QPi were correlated and both predicted 6-month outcome, but QPi was far more sensitive to anaesthetics, which probably confounds its association with intracranial hypertension. The indices are not interchangeable in sedated critically ill patients. ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05567978. Registered 5 October 2022.

article.abstract: Bedside neuromuscular tests are commonly proposed to assess readiness for extubation in critically ill patients. However, when used in unselected populations, their ability to predict clinically relevant outcomes such as extubation failure has been inconsistent. A more targeted use of these tests, restricted to patients in whom neuromuscular weakness is more likely to contribute to weaning failure, may improve their clinical relevance. We conducted a pooled individual patient data analysis of multiple observational cohorts including adult ICU patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation. The primary outcome was extubation failure, defined as reintubation or death within 48 h after extubation. Available neuromuscular assessments included maximal inspiratory pressure (MIP), maximal expiratory pressure (MEP), peak cough flow (PCF), and Medical Research Council (MRC) sum score. Prespecified thresholds were MIP ≤ 30 cmH₂O, MEP ≤ 50 cmH₂O, PCF ≤ 60 L/min, and MRC < 48/60. Associations with extubation failure were assessed in the overall population and according to prior mechanical ventilation duration. Among 494 included patients, 458 had an available extubation outcome and 72 (16%) experienced extubation failure. MIP was available in 230 patients, MEP in 124, PCF in 156, and MRC score in 252. In the overall population, MIP ≤ 30 cmH₂O showed only a borderline association with extubation failure (24% vs. 14%; OR 1.94, 95% CI 0.98 to 3.84; p = 0.06). In patients ventilated for more than 5 days, extubation failure occurred in 33% with MIP ≤ 30 cmH₂O versus 14% with MIP > 30 cmH₂O. After adjustment, MIP ≤ 30 cmH₂O remained associated with extubation failure (adjusted OR 3.52, 95% CI 1.37 to 9.03; p = 0.009). No significant adjusted association was observed for MEP, PCF, or MRC. Neuromuscular tests may have limited prognostic value when applied broadly before extubation. Low MIP appears more informative after prolonged mechanical ventilation, supporting a targeted rather than systematic use of respiratory neuromuscular assessment before extubation.
article.title: Toward targeted assessment of inspiratory muscle weakness before extubation: a pooled individual patient data analysis from multiple observational cohorts in critically ill ventilated patients.

article.abstract: The study examined the effect of daily music therapy on weaning from invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) in the ICU, with a primary focus on weaning duration. Secondary agitation, sedation, and analgesia doses, pain, delirium, and perceived stress after 90 days were assessed. Additionally, total IMV and ICU stay durations and tracheostomy rates were studied. Physiologic parameters were assessed in the music therapy group (MG). The study also aimed to promote the humanization of critical care through a biopsychosocial and creative music therapy approach. Randomized controlled trial with two parallel groups: control group receiving standard care during weaning and MG receiving music therapy additionally. Adult critically ill patients (n = 100) admitted to a general ICU who received IMV for at least 48 hours. MG received daily, individualized music therapy sessions averaging 25 minutes, based on patient needs and musical preferences, which included music relaxation, music listening, and clinical improvisation. No significant difference in weaning duration was observed between groups (p = 0.97). Patients in the MG group showed significant improvements in agitation and sedation levels (Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale) on days 1 and 3 (p = 0.048, 0.005, and 0.024) and a lower percentage required propofol (p = 0.028). No significant difference in perceived pain (Visual Analog Pain Scale). The MG obtained lower Perceived Stress Scale-14 scores (p = 0.24). Additionally, MG significantly reduced tracheostomy rates (14%; p = 0.025). Median total IMV and ICU stay duration were shorter in the MG group, but not significantly (p = 0.206 and 0.203). Heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and oxygenation showed no significant difference before and after music therapy. Music therapy may serve as a nonpharmacological complementary adjunct during weaning by reducing agitation, sedation, and tracheostomy rate. It may potentially decrease perceived stress and IMV and ICU stay durations. Further research is warranted.

article.abstract: To determine the incidence of a significant noninvasive brachial-to-radial arterial pressure gradient (NIBR-APG) and its clinical associations in critically ill patients receiving vasoactive agents. Prospective, multicenter, observational study. Thirteen ICUs in Poland. Adult ICU patients with radial arterial catheters receiving vasoactive agents hospitalized between April 2025 and July 2025. None. Invasive radial mean arterial pressure (MAP) and noninvasive brachial MAP were measured twice and averaged. A NIBR-APG greater than 11 mm Hg was predefined as clinically significant. Baseline characteristics, hemodynamic variables, and outcomes were recorded. Among 303 patients, 49.5% were surgical admissions and 33.3% had septic shock. The median NIBR-APG was 4.5 mm Hg (interquartile range, 0.0-10.0 mm Hg). Fifty-six patients (18.4%) exhibited a NIBR-APG greater than 11 mm Hg. Compared with patients without a significant gradient, these patients received higher norepinephrine-equivalent doses (0.23 vs. 0.10 µg/kg/min), had higher Sequential Organ Failure Assessment scores (11 vs. 10), prolonged capillary refill time (3.0 vs. 2.5 s), and higher lactate concentrations (2.7 vs. 1.3 mmol/L). In multivariable analysis, only vasoactive drug dose was independently associated with NIBR-APG greater than 11 mm Hg (odds ratio, 1.68; 95% CI, 1.12-2.52). ICU mortality was higher in patients with significant gradients (48.0% vs. 30.1%). Nearly one in five critically ill patients receiving vasoactive agents demonstrated a clinically significant NIBR-APG. The presence of this gradient was independently associated with higher vasoactive drug requirements and was accompanied by greater illness severity and higher ICU mortality.

article.abstract: This study evaluated the efficacy of different high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) weaning protocols in critically ill adults. This multicenter, randomized controlled trial was conducted from December 1, 2022, to August 31, 2024, based on the suggested protocol (SLOWH trial). Experts reviewed the trial between October 2, 2024, and April 15, 2025. Randomization was performed by a research coordinator using a sequence of random numbers generated by an independent statistician blinded to both researchers and participants. Adults (≥ 18 yr old) in the ICU who met the weaning criteria after receiving HFNC were included. Among 102 patients from three tertiary care hospitals, 15 were excluded. The remaining patients were randomized into three intervention groups: flow reduction (FR) first, Fio2 reduction (OR) first, or simultaneous reduction (SR). The primary outcome was the HFNC weaning success rate, defined as successful transition to conventional oxygen therapy without the need for HFNC reapplication, noninvasive ventilation, or endotracheal intubation within 24 hours. A total of 87 adults completed the trial (FR, n = 31 [male, 52%]; OR, n = 26 [male, 77%]; SR, n = 30 [male, 53%]). The weaning success rates in the FR, OR, and SR groups were 94%, 81%, and 77%, respectively (p = 0.15). The median [interquartile range] weaning duration was 31.0 hours (29.0-45.8 hr), 29.5 hours (28.0-60.4 hr), and 29.5 hours (26.5-45.0 hr) in the FR, OR, and SR groups, respectively, with no statistically significant difference among groups (p = 0.87). In this randomized trial, no statistically significant differences were observed among the three HFNC weaning strategies in terms of weaning success or duration.

article.abstract: Effective strategies to prevent weaning failure and prolonged invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) in patients at high risk of weaning failure are limited. We evaluated a structured, specialist-led interprofessional weaning program. In this prospective, multicenter, non-randomized interventional study, mechanically ventilated patients were screened 96 h to 11 days after intubation. Patients meeting predefined high-risk criteria received a specialist-led interprofessional weaning program, while a parallel control group was derived from health insurance claims data. The primary outcome was successful weaning at ICU discharge. The primary analysis included 349 intervention patients and 1,768 controls. Successful weaning occurred in 58.3% of intervention patients and 51.7% of controls. In the adjusted primary analysis, the odds ratio for successful weaning was 1.46 (95% CI, 0.99-2.17; P = 0.057), and the difference did not reach statistical significance. In prespecified propensity score-matched analysis, successful weaning occurred in 58.3% of intervention patients and 46.4% of matched controls (OR, 2.90; 95% CI, 1.61-5.24; P < 0.001). An exploratory analysis restricted to ICU survivors also showed higher odds of successful weaning in the intervention group (OR, 2.10; 95% CI, 1.09-4.04; P = 0.026). Overall, 16.3% of intervention patients were transferred to a specialized weaning center. These patients had longer ventilation durations, contributing to a longer overall duration of IMV in the intervention group. The PRiVENT intervention was feasible and successful weaning was numerically more frequent in the intervention group, although the prespecified adjusted primary analysis did not reach statistical significance. These findings suggest a potential benefit of structured, multidisciplinary weaning support. ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05260853, registered on March 2, 2022.

article.abstract: The preferred method of renal-replacement therapy for acute kidney injury in critically ill patients remains uncertain. In this multicenter, open-label, noninferiority trial, we randomly assigned critically ill adults with acute kidney injury who had indications for renal-replacement therapy to undergo intermittent hemodialysis or continuous renal-replacement therapy as the initial treatment. The primary outcome was a major adverse kidney event - defined as death, dependence on renal-replacement therapy, or a serum creatinine concentration more than 25% above the baseline value - by day 90. The trial was stopped early after sequential interim analyses showed a sustained signal of higher mortality with intermittent hemodialysis than with continuous renal-replacement therapy. A total of 554 patients underwent randomization, with 272 patients assigned to undergo intermittent hemodialysis and 282 to undergo continuous renal-replacement therapy; 535 patients (260 in the intermittent group and 275 in the continuous group) were included in the intention-to-treat population. A major adverse kidney event occurred by day 90 in 203 patients (78.1%) in the intermittent group and in 197 patients (71.6%) in the continuous group (adjusted absolute risk difference, 6.28 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -1.22 to 13.79). Death by day 90 occurred in 164 patients (63.1%) and in 147 patients (53.5%), respectively. Kaplan-Meier mortality estimates at day 90 were 63.3% and 53.6% (hazard ratio, 1.30; 95% CI, 1.04 to 1.63). The most common complication potentially related to acute kidney injury or renal-replacement therapy was hypotension, which occurred in 179 patients (68.8%) in the intermittent group and in 183 patients (66.5%) in the continuous group. Among critically ill patients with acute kidney injury who had indications for renal-replacement therapy, intermittent hemodialysis as the initial treatment approach was not shown to be noninferior to continuous renal-replacement therapy with respect to major adverse kidney events by day 90 and was associated with higher mortality. (Funded by the French Ministry of Health; ICRAKI ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06032884.).

article.abstract: Given multifactorial mechanisms driving vasodilation in septic shock, there is a strong physiological rationale for early initiation of multiple vasopressors (angiotensin II, vasopressin and norepinephrine) with complementary mechanisms of action. Such an approach could more effectively counteract the complex pathophysiological processes characteristic of septic shock. Here we tested the physiological and clinical effects of an early multimodal vasopressor strategy in patients with septic shock. We randomly assigned patients with septic shock receiving ≥ 0.15 µg/kg/min of norepinephrine base to either intervention (early multimodal vasopressor administration: angiotensin II, vasopressin, and norepinephrine) group or control (classic stepwise vasopressor administration: norepinephrine dose increase followed by vasopressin and then by angiotensin II or other vasopressors) group. The primary outcome was change in plasma renin concentrations. This phase II trial was not powered to detect differences in mortality. A total of 79 patients were included (intervention group: n = 38, control group: n = 41). We observed a faster decline in plasma renin concentrations (2.61% per hour vs. 1.67% per hour; p = 0.015) and lactate concentrations (1.53% per hour vs. 1.01% per hour; p = 0.006) during the first 72 h in the intervention group compared to the control group. At 72 h, Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score was reduced by 3 points in the intervention group vs. 0 in the control group (p = 0.018). In the additional non-prespecified analyses, norepinephrine equivalent (NEE) dose decreased at a similar rate in the intervention and control groups over 72 h (- 5.41% per hour vs. -5.19% per hour; p = 0.47), whereas over the first 24 h, NEE dose decreased significantly faster in the intervention group (- 6.87% per hour vs. -3.03% per hour; p < 0.0004). The incidence of tachyarrhythmias was significantly lower in the intervention group (15.6% vs. 68.6%; p < 0.01). Intensive care unit mortality (26.3% vs. 41.5%; RR 0.635; 95% CI 0.33 to 1.21; p = 0.235) and 28-day mortality (36.8% vs. 46.3%; RR 0.795; 95% CI 0.47 to 1.35; p = 0.494) were similar. Early multimodal vasopressor therapy with Ang II, vasopressin and norepinephrine in patients with septic shock demonstrated promising physiological effects. These findings provide a rationale for a larger trial to assess whether early multimodal vasopressor therapy improves patient-centered outcomes. ClinicalTrials.gov ID: NCT06155812. URL: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06155812?term=NCT06155812&rank=1 . Trial registration date: 4 December 2023.
